3. FIR No.255/2024 came to be registered by the appellant-complainant 
with the Paranda Police Station, District Dharashiv on 26.11.2024 
against accused-respondent No.1 herein and others in respect of 
alleged commission of offenses punishable under Sections 118 (1), 
115(1), 189(2), 189(4), 190, 191(2), 191(3), 333, 324(4), 76, 351(3) 
and 352 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and under Sections 
3(1)(o), 3(1)(r), 3(1)(s), 3(1)(w)(i) of the Scheduled Castes and 
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989. 
3.1 The relevant and material part of the contents of the said FIR 
is extracted below.
“Today on 25.11.2024 at around 11:00 AM, while I and 
my mother Mohini were at home, Bahubali Masalkar, 
a peon from the Gram Panchayat Office, Kapilapuri, 
came in front of my house and started abusing us, 
asking why we did not vote in yesterday’s assembly 
elections as we had asked. At that time, I tried to tell 
him that voting was my only concern, but he abused 
me and then rushed at me. At that time, we got into 
a fight. After that we got into a fight. After that he

Then at 11:20 in the morning, my village’s known, 
namely Rajkumar Jain, Jaykumar Jain, Bharatesh 
Awani, Jayghosh Jain, Kishore Awani, Vaibhav 
Awani, Nabiraj Awani, Bahubali Masalkar, Jitendra 
Wasgadekar, Anil Wasgadekar, Ranjit Rajkumar Jain, 
Jagdish Jain, all residents of Kapilapuri (all Jains), 
came in front of our house. At that time, Rajkumar 
Jain said to me, “Mangtyano, you have become much 
arrogant”, you are staying in the village and voting 
against me, so he hit me on the head and back with 
an iron rod.” At that time, I fell down. After that, Kishore 
Jain and Vaibhav Awani entered my house, pushed 
my mother Mohini and aunt Rekha, grabbed the 
saree of mother Mohini and pulled it, threatened that

Wasgadekar, Anil Wasgadekar, Ranjeet Rajkumar 
Jain, Jagdish Jain, all residents of Kapilapuri, angry 
that I voted against them in yesterday’s assembly 
elections, even though they knew that I and my family 
belongs to the Matang community, they abused us in

I am giving my above statement with full of my

3.2 What is narrated in the FIR disclosed certain manifest aspects. 
On 25.11.2024 in the morning, the respondent-accused along 
with others went to the house of the appellant and standing 
outside and in front of appellant’s house stated to the appellant 
“Mangtyano, you have become much arrogant, you are staying 
in the village and voting against me”. The appellant was attacked 
with an iron rod. The mother and aunt of the appellant were 
addressed with the same set of words as above and that they 
all were beaten with the iron rod and were punched inflicting 
internal injuries, the Mangalsutra of the mother fell somewhere 
in the scuffle. The accused had in their hands petrol bottles 
and were repeatedly shouting and threatening that they would 
burn the house of the appellant. The injured appellant lodged 
the FIR from the hospital.
3.3 The evident reason for this incident was animosity generated in 
the mind of the accused in respect of appellant’s act of not voting 
in favour of particular candidate in the assembly elections which 
had concluded on the previous day. The exhibition of enmity 
by the accused, their utterances as above and the conduct of 
beating the appellant and hurling castiest abuses and threats 
were in public view, outside the house of the appellant. The 
appellant belonged to the Scheduled Caste community whose 
caste was “Mang” or “Matang”; whereas the respondent accused 
was not the member of the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe 
community. He hailed from ‘Jain’ community. 
3.4 While rejecting the prayer of respondent-accused for anticipatory 
bail, the Additional Sessions Judge, Paranda recorded findings 
in paragraph 8 of his order inter alia that there was a specific 
allegation against the accused and that the accused had 
abused the complainant by referring to his caste, that the 
caste certificate confirmed that the complainant-informant 
belonged to the Scheduled Caste community and further that 
the incident was witnessed by independent witnesses. On the 
basis of statements in the FIR and the material available, the 
court concluded that the ingredients of the offences punishable

Kiran v. Rajkumar Jivraj Jain & Anr.
under Section 3 of the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes 
(Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (hereinafter referred to as 
“the SC/ST Act”) as alleged were made out. 
3.5 When the order rejecting the anticipatory bail was challenged 
before the High Court by the accused, the High Court took the 
view to record that there were inconsistencies in the prosecution 
story as could be gathered from the account of eye-witnesses. 
According to the High Court, the entire prosecution case 
appeared to be exaggerated and false. What weighed with the 
High Court was also the aspect that the incident took place 
immediately after the declaration of results of the assembly 
elections, therefore, it had political overtures. Resting on such 
considerations, the High Court concluded that the appellant was 
falsely implicated. Further referring to the nature of the injuries 
and allegations, the High Court granted anticipatory bail. 
4. Mr. Amol Nirmalkumar Suryawanshi, learned counsel appearing for 
the appellant-herein assailed the judgment and order of the High 
Court to submit that the High Court not only misdirected itself in 
exercise of the discretion to grant bail to respondent No.1, but it 
plainly overlooked the provisions of Section 18 of the SC/ST Act. 
Highlighting the contents of and the allegations in the FIR, it was 
submitted that the accused used abusive language referring to 
caste and the appellant who was the member of the Scheduled 
Caste community was thereby subjected to derogation and insult. 
The appellant was intimidated and his mother and aunt were also 
abused with castiest slur and were threatened. Learned counsel for 
the appellant further submitted that the castiest slur and the castiest 
abuse employed against the appellant clearly made out the offence 
under Section 3 of the SC/ST Act as alleged and since the offence 
was prima facie committed, the pre-arrest bail could not have been 
granted by the High Court in view of the provision of Section 18 of 
the Act. 
4.1 Learned counsel for the appellant relied on the decision of Vilas 
Pandurang Pawar vs. State of Maharashtra 1 to submit that 
at the stage of the consideration of grant of bail or otherwise, 
the High Court was not expected to conduct a mini trial. It

was submitted that the reasoning of the High Court was not 
acceptable. Regarding bar created by virtue of Section 18 of the 
SC/ST Act, learned counsel pressed into service the decision 
of this Court in Prathvi Raj Chauhan vs. Union of India2. 
4.2 On the other hand, learned counsel for respondent No.1 seeking 
to defend the order of the High Court, submitted that Section 
18 of the SC/ST Act did not create an absolute bar to grant 
anticipatory bail. He proceeded to submit that in subsequent 
decision of this Court in Shajan Skaria vs. The State of Kerala 
& Anr.3, it was observed that the court needed to undertake an 
exercise to find out whether there was a prima facie substance 
in the allegations. According to learned counsel for respondent 
No.1, the allegations in the FIR were made for the sake of 
making and were out of anger regarding casting of vote in the 
assembly elections. He tried to submit that it was wrong to give 
a castiest colour to the allegations to conclude that any offence 
under the SC/ST Act was committed by the accused. 
4.3 The respondent-State of Maharashtra filed the counter affidavit 
and opposed the grant of pre-arrest bail to respondent No.1 
accused by emphasising the operational ambit of Section 18 
of the SC/ST Act. It was highlighted that when prima facie 
material existed in the form of allegations in the FIR and other 
attendant factual aspects, the respondent No.1 could not have 
been granted the anticipatory bail by the High Court.

case_facts.text: The High Court of Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad, by judgment and order dated 29.04.2025 in Criminal Appeal No. 201 of 2025, granted pre-arrest bail to respondent No. 1 under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
The Additional Sessions Judge, Paranda had earlier refused anticipatory bail to respondent No. 1.

FIR No. 255/2024 was registered at Paranda Police Station, District Dharashiv, on 26.11.2024 against respondent No. 1 and others for offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

The complainant alleged that on 25.11.2024 at about 11:00 AM, Bahubali Masalkar came to his house, abused him and his mother Mohini, and asked why they had not voted as requested in the assembly election.
The complainant alleged that Bahubali Masalkar rushed at him, causing a fight, and then left the place.

The complainant alleged that around 11:20 AM, Rajkumar Jain, Jaykumar Jain, Bharatesh Awani, Jayghosh Jain, Kishore Awani, Vaibhav Awani, Nabiraj Awani, Bahubali Masalkar, Jitendra Wasgadekar, Anil Wasgadekar, Ranjit Rajkumar Jain, and Jagdish Jain came to his house.
The complainant alleged that Rajkumar Jain abused him using caste-based words, said he had become arrogant and was voting against them, and struck him on the head and back with an iron rod.
The complainant alleged that he fell down after being hit with the iron rod.

The complainant alleged that Kishore Jain and Vaibhav Awani entered his house, pushed his mother Mohini and aunt Rekha, pulled Mohini's saree, threatened to burn their houses and not let them stay in the village, and beat them with an iron rod and punches causing internal injuries.
The complainant alleged that a one-tola gold mangalsutra belonging to his mother fell during the scuffle.
The complainant alleged that the attackers damaged household utensils and caused total damage to household items.
The complainant alleged that his friend Yashwant Bodre came to resolve the dispute and was beaten on the left hand and back with an iron rod by Rajkumar Jain.
The complainant alleged that some of the assailants had petrol bottles and repeatedly threatened to burn his house and not let them stay in the village.
The complainant alleged that villagers Avinash Masgude, Appa Masgude, and Omkar Mane came and rescued them from the assailants.
The complainant alleged that after approaching Paranda Police Station, he was given a medical treatment letter and sent to Paranda Sub-District Hospital for treatment.
The complainant stated that he and his family belong to the Matang community and that the accused abused them in caste terms because they had voted against them in the assembly election.
The complainant alleged that the incident occurred in public view outside his house.
The complainant belonged to the Scheduled Caste community and the accused belonged to the Jain community.
The Additional Sessions Judge, Paranda recorded that there was a specific allegation that the accused abused the complainant by referring to his caste.
The Additional Sessions Judge, Paranda recorded that the caste certificate confirmed that the complainant belonged to the Scheduled Caste community.
The Additional Sessions Judge, Paranda recorded that the incident was witnessed by independent witnesses.
The Additional Sessions Judge concluded that the ingredients of the offences under Section 3 of the SC/ST Act, as alleged, were made out.
The High Court found inconsistencies in the prosecution story from the account of eye-witnesses and considered the prosecution case exaggerated and false.
The High Court considered that the incident occurred immediately after declaration of the assembly election results and had political overtones.
The High Court concluded that the appellant was falsely implicated and granted anticipatory bail after considering the nature of the injuries and allegations.

### Legal Theory
May it please the Court, I strongly oppose this application for anticipatory bail. Section 438 CrPC is an extraordinary remedy, not a matter of routine. The record here discloses far more than a simple dispute: the FIR alleges that a group of named persons came to the complainant’s house, abused him and his mother in caste terms, assaulted him with an iron rod, pushed and beat the women in the house, threatened to burn the house with petrol bottles, damaged household property, and attacked the person who came to rescue them. These are serious allegations attracting IPC Sections 323, 324, 352, 426, 427, 448, 451, 452, 504, 506, and, on the complainant’s version, Section 3 of the SC/ST Act.

### Submissions
1. The Additional Sessions Judge has already recorded that there was specific caste abuse, that the complainant belongs to a Scheduled Caste community, and that independent witnesses witnessed the incident. In **Srikant Upadhyay v. State of Bihar**, the Supreme Court held that anticipatory bail is exceptional and should not be granted as a matter of course; it also emphasized that a person facing serious criminal process must submit to the authority of law. That principle applies with full force here.
2. Custodial interrogation is necessary for concrete reasons: the incident involves multiple named assailants, an iron rod, alleged petrol bottles, and damage to household property. The prosecution must confront the applicant with the specific role attributed to him, identify the roles of the co-accused, and secure the truth of the threats and assault. Further, the complainant, his mother, aunt, and a rescuer are all named in the narrative, so witness protection is a live concern if the applicant is granted pre-arrest protection.
3. In view of the gravity of the offence, statutory presumptions, and the necessity of custodial interrogation, the prosecution humbly prays that this Anticipatory Bail application be rejected.
- **Section 438 CrPC**: anticipatory bail; an exceptional pre-arrest remedy.
- **Section 167 CrPC**: investigative custody framework, relevant where effective interrogation is required during investigation.
- **IPC Section 323**: voluntarily causing hurt — requires proof of hurt and voluntary infliction.
- **IPC Section 324**: voluntarily causing hurt by dangerous weapons or means — here, the alleged **iron rod** is the relevant dangerous weapon.
- **IPC Section 352**: assault or criminal force otherwise than on grave provocation.
- **IPC Section 354**: assault/criminal force to woman with intent to outrage modesty — relevant to the alleged pulling of Mohini’s saree, if pressed on facts.
- **IPC Section 426 / 427**: mischief and mischief causing damage — relevant to the alleged damage to utensils and household items.
- **IPC Section 448 / 451 / 452**: house-trespass, trespass to commit offence, and trespass after preparation for hurt/assault/wrongful restraint — relevant because the FIR alleges entry into the house with iron rod and petrol bottles.
- **IPC Section 504**: intentional insult with intent to provoke breach of peace — relevant to caste abuse and threats.
- **IPC Section 506**: criminal intimidation — relevant to threats to burn the house and expel the family from the village.
- **IPC Section 509**: words/gestures intended to insult the modesty of a woman — potentially relevant to the allegations concerning Mohini.
- **Section 3 of the SC/ST Act**: the record shows allegations of caste-based abuse against a Scheduled Caste complainant in public view.
The FIR in this case is not limited to a simple quarrel. It alleges that on 25.11.2024, after the election results, a group including the present respondent came to the complainant’s house, abused him and his mother in caste terms, assaulted him with an iron rod, entered the house, manhandled the women, threatened to burn the house with petrol bottles, damaged household articles, and beat a friend who came to intervene. The Additional Sessions Judge found specific caste abuse, SC status of the complainant, and independent witnesses; these findings directly support the conclusion that the ingredients of the SC/ST allegation were prima facie made out.
4. The prosecution’s need for custody is not generic here. The case involves **multiple named assailants**, **an iron rod**, **alleged petrol bottles**, and **damage to household property**. Custodial interrogation is necessary to confront the applicant with the role attributed to him and to identify the part played by each co-accused in the group attack, the source and use of the weapon, and the circumstances of the threats to burn the house. Because the incident allegedly occurred in public view and independent witnesses are referenced, the applicant being on pre-arrest bail risks influencing witnesses and obstructing a free and fair investigation. The complainant and his family also allege threats to their residence and safety, which makes protection of witnesses a live concern.
5. The High Court’s view that the prosecution story is exaggerated cannot override the FIR’s detailed allegations at the anticipatory bail stage, especially where the record already reflects a caste-based insult, physical assault, and intimidation. On the facts as recorded, this is precisely the kind of case where Section 438 CrPC should not be used to neutralize investigation.

transcript.speaker: defense
transcript.content:
### Legal Theory
The prosecution version discloses a politically coloured group scuffle with allegations that are serious but materially contested; at the anticipatory bail stage, the record shows no medical report or other objective proof on file, and the prosecution’s case on specific overt acts, caste intent, and witness reliability remains vulnerable to challenge under the limited material presently on record.

### Submissions
1. The prosecution relies heavily on the FIR narrative and the Sessions Court’s prima facie view, but the High Court has already noted inconsistencies in the eye-witness account and treated the prosecution story as exaggerated and false [fact_23], [fact_25]. The alleged incident also occurred immediately after declaration of election results and had political overtones [fact_24], which materially weakens the inference of a deliberate caste-driven assault and supports the defense submission that the dispute may have arisen from a sudden political flashpoint rather than a premeditated criminal design [fact_4], [fact_16].
2. The record before the court does not contain a medical report, injury certificate, MLC, or hospital report; it only reflects that the complainant was given a medical treatment letter and sent to the Sub-District Hospital [fact_15]. The prosecution has failed to produce on record any forensic report or seizure material regarding the alleged iron rod, petrol bottles, or damaged articles, so the asserted seriousness of IPC 324 and IPC 427/BNS-linked allegations remains uncorroborated by objective evidence in the present record.
3. On the statutory ingredients, the allegations do not by themselves establish the requisite mens rea for every invoked provision. For IPC 504 and IPC 506, mere abusive words or threats in a heated election-related confrontation are not enough unless intentional provocation or a real criminal intimidation to cause alarm is shown with clarity [fact_4], [fact_13], [fact_24]. For IPC 324, the prosecution must still prove voluntary causing of hurt by a dangerous weapon, yet the record presently lacks medical evidence and independent corroboration of the precise role of the applicant [fact_7], [fact_15]. For the SC/ST Act allegation, although the Sessions Court noted caste abuse and SC status [fact_19], [fact_20], [fact_22], the High Court’s finding of inconsistencies and exaggeration [fact_23], [fact_25] creates a substantial doubt on whether the alleged caste abuse was the dominant animus or whether the episode was primarily a political altercation.

arguments: The prosecution relies heavily on the FIR narrative and the Sessions Court’s prima facie view, but the High Court has already noted inconsistencies in the eye-witness account and treated the prosecution story as exaggerated and false [fact_23], [fact_25]. The alleged incident also occurred immediately after declaration of election results and had political overtones [fact_24], which materially weakens the inference of a deliberate caste-driven assault and supports the defense submission that the dispute may have arisen from a sudden political flashpoint rather than a premeditated criminal design [fact_4], [fact_16].

The record before the court does not contain a medical report, injury certificate, MLC, or hospital report; it only reflects that the complainant was given a medical treatment letter and sent to the Sub-District Hospital [fact_15]. The prosecution has failed to produce on record any forensic report or seizure material regarding the alleged iron rod, petrol bottles, or damaged articles, so the asserted seriousness of IPC 324 and IPC 427/BNS-linked allegations remains uncorroborated by objective evidence in the present record.

On the statutory ingredients, the allegations do not by themselves establish the requisite mens rea for every invoked provision. For IPC 504 and IPC 506, mere abusive words or threats in a heated election-related confrontation are not enough unless intentional provocation or a real criminal intimidation to cause alarm is shown with clarity [fact_4], [fact_13], [fact_24]. For IPC 324, the prosecution must still prove voluntary causing of hurt by a dangerous weapon, yet the record presently lacks medical evidence and independent corroboration of the precise role of the applicant [fact_7], [fact_15]. For the SC/ST Act allegation, although the Sessions Court noted caste abuse and SC status [fact_19], [fact_20], [fact_22], the High Court’s finding of inconsistencies and exaggeration [fact_23], [fact_25] creates a substantial doubt on whether the alleged caste abuse was the dominant animus or whether the episode was primarily a political altercation.

verdict.reasoning:
The record does not show any Section 82 proclamation, warrant non-compliance, or other absconding conduct, so the Paragraph 24 exception for jurisdictional abuse or malicious process does not apply. The FIR contains serious allegations, including caste abuse, assault with an iron rod, and threats to burn the house, but the present material is still largely uncorroborated by medical or forensic proof and does not demonstrate that custodial interrogation is indispensable. Individual roles are mixed and attributed to multiple co-accused, with the principal overt acts assigned to others rather than a clearly isolated role for the present applicant. In these circumstances, anticipatory bail can be granted with conditions, without expressing any view on guilt.

factors.finding: The allegations against respondent No. 1 are serious, but the record before this Court remains largely FIR-based, with no medical report, forensic material, or seizure proof on file to show that custodial interrogation is indispensable at this stage.

As to individual role, the FIR attributes the specific iron-rod assault to Rajkumar Jain, the house-entry and assault on the women to Kishore Jain and Vaibhav Awani, and the initial vote-related quarrel to Bahubali Masalkar, so the present applicant’s precise overt act is not established with comparable clarity on the present record.

The Paragraph 24 exception to the absconding/proclamation line of authority is not attracted because there is no Section 82 proclamation, no warrant history, and no showing of jurisdictional abuse or malicious process warranting refusal on that ground.

The Sessions Court’s adverse prima facie view on caste abuse and independent witnesses exists, but the High Court’s own assessment of inconsistencies, exaggeration, and political overtones supports a cautious pre-arrest protection rather than incarceration before trial.
